The top of the `source` resource indicates which places to edit for a new attribute:

> * The IDL and content attributes for the relevant elements
> * element and attribute indexes

In this case IDL would not be changed as this is a parser-driven attribute, similar to `<html manifest>` (which is [now gone](https://github.com/whatwg/html/commit/e4330d510a1d05e1f5f84707c9d6dcec97db94b8)), but it does need to be listed in the other places and have a description in the `template` element section.

Sure, the simplest approach is to hook into where template element's start tag is parsed, and instead of inserting the template element to its parent, create a template element with a shadow root for the parent as its document fragment. Still push the template element to the stack of open so that all the checks for closing template, etc... will work same as a regular template element does. Generally, the use case is to hold useful HTML (now including declarative Shadow DOM) in a template, and be able to stamp out copies of that content.

I chatted with @rniwa about this and I think he has a good point that this is a bit odd. For the HTML parser we're essentially using `<template shadow...>` as a macro to instantiate shadow trees and we preserve some of that state for serialization. But making it affect normal DOM operations as well turns it into a strange API whereby it's no longer just a parser macro. I tend to agree that if we want to support such cases we should offer a specialized API that would maybe also work if you put shadow trees in `template`'s contents yourself. (That specialized API can also be a future entry point for templating, where we also ran into needing something like that for the `template` element.)

> For the HTML parser we're essentially using `<template shadow...>` as a macro to instantiate shadow trees and we preserve some of that state for serialization. But making it affect normal DOM operations as well turns it into a strange API whereby it's no longer just a parser macro.

I think the weirdness comes from the fact regular shadow trees are not cloned when you call importNode or cloneNode but declarative shadow trees are.

One way to rectify this weirdness might be to add an independent flag like "cloneable" as an argument to attachShadow. Declarative shadow DOM will implicitly set this flag to true by default (or maybe it could be explicit?).

Alternatively, we could introduce a new option dictionary like {includeShadowRoots: true} to allow cloning of shadow trees, and authors would have to use that API to clone shadow trees. This isn't so ideal because the author / maintainer of a component doesn't get a choice on whether cloning is allowed or not. So maybe we'd need cloneable flag in this case as well.

> > For the HTML parser we're essentially using `<template shadow...>` as a macro to instantiate shadow trees and we preserve some of that state for serialization. But making it affect normal DOM operations as well turns it into a strange API whereby it's no longer just a parser macro.

> I think the weirdness comes from the fact regular shadow trees are not cloned when you call importNode or cloneNode but declarative shadow trees are.
> 
> One way to rectify this weirdness might be to add an independent flag like "cloneable" as an argument to attachShadow. Declarative shadow DOM will implicitly set this flag to true by default (or maybe it could be explicit?).

I do see this point. The reason I implemented it this way was for web compat - we obviously can't just start cloning shadow roots everywhere. I really like the idea of adding an explicit flag like `cloneable` on `attachShadow()`, and having it default to `true` for declarative shadow DOM. This way, the change is web compatible, and there's a parity between imperative and declarative shadow roots. Plus we don't have to introduce another cloning method. There's already enough confusion between `cloneNode()` and `importNode()`, I'd hate to make that worse.

> You're free to keep insisting that but the likely outcome of that will be that this PR will never get merged.

> I'm saying that we need to exclude it for the purpose of merging this spec PR into HTML/DOM in near term since there is no consensus to add it.

This discussion started 3 years ago and stalled for 2 years. I'm very glad folks have come back to work on it, but I don't think there's pressure to rush it to land immediately, is there?

My rationale for excluding it is:

* `DOMParser` is not an API we plan to extend. It has been kept around because it cannot be removed, but it's very far from a modern API. Giving web developers the impression this is the way to go is shortsighted. I don't think we should tell them to use this API today and `setHTML()` (and friends) six months to a year from now. We should be handing web developers solutions that last, not make them jump in circles.
* This is by far not the main use case for this feature.
* It's rather weird to refuse to specify the part that has two interoperable implementations.

To pick an extreme example, if we add a different new HTML tag `<foobar>` to the spec, are you supportive of also disallowing `DOMParser` (and `innerHTML` and `outerHTML` etc) from parsing that tag?
